TITLE: Rinse Water Control Systems for Metal Finishing

Rinse Water Control Systems for Metal Finishing | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Manufacturing Field note · Metal finishing · September 30, 2026 Start with what the rinse loop already knows. A finishing line can have a good conductivity controller and still lack a clear account of which production change increased water use or sent more chemistry toward treatment. The first job is to join the evidence already there. This is a proposed operating study, not a measured AquaMesh result at a metal finishing plant. What is established Conductivity control has a real job. An EPA Region 9 metal finishing project describes the basic rinse loop: a conductivity sensor and analyzer open a solenoid valve when the rinse reaches a set point, then close it after the reading falls below a deadband. The goal is adequate rinsing without constant fresh water flow. The same report recommends tracking set points, bath conditions and rejected parts when adjusting the system. The EPA example predates today's software, but its control principle matters. A new platform should not pretend that water savings begin with a novel probe if a conductivity controller, countercurrent rinse or dragout reduction can already address the problem. EPA's pollution prevention manual also describes flow restriction, pH and conductivity control, and dragout reduction as established options. What changed this week Modern automation makes the existing evidence easier to use. In a September 28, 2026 WEFTEC announcement , Schneider Electric described upgrades across PLC security, open automation, connected data and water management software. Schneider says its EcoStruxure Water Advisor and AVEVA CONNECT offerings bring together operational data and analytics. Those are substantial incumbent capabilities. An AquaMesh proposal has to begin by documenting what the facility's PLC, SCADA, historian, water treatment program and service provider already cover. For a rinse line, the missing question may be operational rather than computational: when conductivity rises, was it the expected result of a particular rack, bath concentration or changeover, a valve problem, a drifted probe, or a genuine process upset? A conductivity trend alone cannot distinguish all of those causes. That is a hypothesis to test at the facility, not a claim that a named vendor's system cannot solve it. A practical test Follow one event from part to treatment. 1 Define the decision Choose one rinse tank and one action the shift team can approve: inspect a valve, check a probe, adjust a set point within a qualified window, change a dragout practice, or hold a batch for quality review. Keep product quality and discharge requirements as hard constraints. 2 Align existing timestamps Put rack or barrel movements, bath condition, conductivity, valve state, makeup flow, reject records and wastewater treatment data on the same timeline. Separate normal load changes from events that would justify intervention. The EPA metal finishing project specifically ties set point review to bath condition and rejects; that is the starting evidence, not an optional afterthought. 3 State what remains unknown If installed measurements show a change but cannot identify the physical condition needed for the chosen decision, define the missing variable and sampling location. Test any proposed optical measurement against a relevant laboratory method across real bath and rinse conditions. Do not infer a metal concentration, compliance result or validated spectral performance from an uncalibrated signal. 4 Verify the response After an operator approved action, check rinse conductivity and flow alongside part quality and downstream treatment evidence. A lower water reading alone is not a win if it increases rejects or dragin to the next bath. AquaMesh's proposed role is to connect the event, likely cause, authorized action and verification. The installed controller still performs its control duty; new sensing has to earn its place through a defined comparison. Sources and scope Opened primary sources. U.S. EPA Region 9, Reducing Rinse Water Use With Conductivity Control Systems , December 1996. Describes the control loop and a facility evaluation; historical evidence, not a claim about current installations. U.S. EPA, Pollution Prevention for the Metal Finishing Industry , rinse water and dragout control guidance. Schneider Electric, WEFTEC 2026 announcement , September 28, 2026. Vendor description of its own automation and software scope. The event study and proposed AquaMesh workflow above are inference. No customer savings, sensor accuracy or vendor gap is asserted. Find the rinse decision your data cannot explain. Start with the controller and process records already in use, then validate any remaining measurement gap. Industrial Water Reuse Monitoring Guide | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Industrial water Field note · Industrial water reuse · September 29, 2026 Match the signal to the failure you need to catch. A reuse line can have plenty of measurements and still leave an operator without an answer. The starting question is specific: which developing condition would change a routing, treatment or maintenance decision while there is still time to act? This is an operating framework, not a report of AquaMesh performance at a customer site. Requirements vary with water source, end use and permit. Start with the use One reuse system, several different questions. A flow balance can show that recovered water is being produced without reaching a use point. It cannot establish that the water is suitable for that use. A quality reading at the treatment outlet can show a process change, but it does not identify which valve or demand change caused a routing loss. The operator needs both views on the same timeline. The end use sets the required treatment and monitoring context. As one example, EPA’s September 2026 summary of California rules for recycled municipal wastewater distinguishes industrial cooling that creates mist from cooling that does not; its table also identifies continuous turbidity monitoring for certain disinfected tertiary uses and separate coliform sampling. That state-specific summary is not a universal specification for every industrial process water loop. EPA: California industrial reuse summary . Choose the evidence What does each measurement actually establish? 1 Flow, level and valve state Use these with production and demand records to locate a water balance or routing problem. Check meter health and whether measurements represent the same operating interval before calling the difference a loss. 2 Pressure and turbidity Use treatment equipment status and appropriate quality tags to flag a filtration change. An alarm should point to the affected train, its operating mode and the approved response. A turbidity signal is not a direct microbial measurement. 3 Laboratory and microbiological evidence Keep the prescribed sampling and methods authoritative. A 2026 Water Research Foundation project tested automated ATP monitoring at a full-scale non-potable reuse facility during normal operation and simulated treatment failures. Its public abstract reports detection of simulated membrane failures within minutes and describes ATP as a complement to conventional laboratory monitoring. That result is evidence for the studied application, not validation of an optical probe or a substitute for a site’s compliance method. WRF project 5319 . 4 Composition at a decision point If the available tags show that a stream changed but cannot distinguish the physical condition that determines whether it can be reused, define that gap precisely. A targeted spectral measurement might be tested for a suitable chemical or organic signature, with paired laboratory samples, a defined range, fouling checks and false-alarm review. It must not be presented as a pathogen test or as a validated concentration before that validation exists. A testable operating study Work backward from the decision. For a hypothetical reuse train, pick one event that would trigger a hold, diversion, inspection or return to service under the plant’s own procedures. Reconstruct the event using timestamped SCADA and historian tags, equipment and maintenance records, production demand, and the laboratory sample collection and result times. Include normal runs for comparison. At each point, write down what the operator knew then , not what became clear days later. Test whether the existing instruments give enough warning and a likely cause. If they do, improve the decision route and verification. If they do not, specify the missing physical observation and test a sensor at that location. Route any proposed response for operator approval, then check the downstream trend and reference sample against the expected result. A useful alert names the condition, evidence, owner and action window. The measurement earns its place when it improves that decision and the result can be checked. Sources and scope Primary sources. U.S. EPA, California industrial reuse summary , updated September 9, 2026. This summarizes state rules and directs readers to the state for current requirements. The Water Research Foundation, project 5319 , report dated July 21, 2026. This article uses the public project abstract; the full report requires subscriber access. The sequence of decisions and the hypothetical study above are AquaMesh’s interpretation. No customer outcome or sensor performance is asserted. Find the decision your plant cannot make soon enough. AquaMesh starts with existing plant data and adds sensing where a specific visibility gap remains. Liquid Cooling Water Quality Decisions | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Data centers Field note · Liquid cooling · September 29, 2026 Separate the loop before the alarm. A water quality alert has little value until the team knows which cooling circuit it describes, who owns that circuit, and what action the evidence supports. This is an operating framework based on published guidance, not a report of AquaMesh performance at a data center. First boundary Facility water and server coolant are different systems. An ASHRAE TC 9.9 white paper distinguishes facility water systems (FWS) from technology cooling systems (TCS), which a coolant distribution unit commonly separates. The paper warns that applying the quality specification for one loop to the other can either impose needless cost on the facility side or leave the IT side at risk. It also notes that ownership may differ between facilities staff, the IT owner, equipment provider and service provider. Before setting a threshold, draw that boundary on the plant diagram. Identify the sample point, fluid, treatment program, materials, control owner and equipment manufacturer's requirements. A signal on a cooling tower does not establish the condition inside a separated server loop. Nor does a server-side result alone identify a tower fault. Existing coverage Use each signal for the question it answers. 1 Thermal and hydraulic tags Trend supply and return temperature, flow, pressure differential, pump and valve state, filter differential pressure, and load by operating mode. These records can localize a heat transfer or flow problem. They do not, by themselves, identify its chemical cause. The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory liquid cooling controls guide describes the data inputs and ownership choices involved. 2 Conductivity, pH and turbidity ASHRAE describes these as an intermediate online monitoring option, with cost and risk determining whether it is warranted. Conductivity responds to dissolved ionic content; it is not a specific contaminant assay. The USGS conductance reference explains that the reading depends on the types and amounts of dissolved substances and temperature. Interpret a change alongside makeup water, dosing, temperature compensation and the correct loop's specification. 3 Samples and equipment guidance Maintain the sampling and analysis required by the fluid and equipment providers. ASHRAE's paper calls for a monitoring frequency and an agreed response to out-of-range values; it explicitly retains periodic bacteria samples. A conductivity, pH or turbidity trend does not replace those tests or prove biological safety. 4 A defined missing observation If existing tags flag a change but cannot distinguish the physical state that would change an operator decision, write down that missing variable and the point of measurement. Targeted spectral sensing could be evaluated for a suitable signature with paired reference samples, interference and fouling checks, and false-alarm review. No spectral result should be treated as a validated concentration, bacteria test or corrosion-rate measurement without application-specific validation. Operating test Reconstruct the decision at the time it mattered. Choose one historical water quality or cooling event. Align the existing BMS or historian trends with lab sample collection time, dosing and maintenance records, operating mode, and CDU status. Ask which loop changed first, whether the evidence identified a likely cause, and who had authority to isolate, sample, inspect or hold equipment under the site's procedures. Compare with a normal run before declaring an anomaly. Then define a prospective test: a condition that triggers an operator-reviewed action, an acceptable false-alarm rate, and the downstream signal or sample that would verify the response. ASHRAE emphasizes an agreed plan for out-of-range results; this is where monitoring becomes a decision rather than another chart. Start with the loop, the owner and the response window. Add an instrument only when the evidence required for that decision is missing from the installed controls and sampling program. Sources and scope Primary references. ASHRAE TC 9.9, Water-Cooled Servers: Common Designs, Components, and Processes , especially water quality and monitoring sections. Published guidance, not an AquaMesh validation. U.S. Geological Survey, Specific Electrical Conductance , measurement basis for conductivity. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Liquid Cooling Controls Team white paper , control system data inputs. The historical review and prospective test are AquaMesh's proposed method. They are not a claim of a particular site's results or a tested AquaSpectra performance level. Find the decision your cooling data cannot make soon enough. AquaMesh starts with installed controls and samples, then tests sensing against a specific visibility gap. TITLE: UV/Vis Spectral Sensing and AI for Industrial Water
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/insights/spectral-sensing-ai-industrial-water.html

UV/Vis Spectral Sensing and AI for Industrial Water | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Technical guide · Process measurement · 7 October 2026 How spectral sensing and AI work together in industrial water. Spectral instruments can reveal a change in a process stream. SCADA, production records and lab results explain what the plant was doing when it happened. An operational model becomes useful when it joins those two views and gives an operator a testable decision. Engineering framework, not a report of a validated AquaMesh industrial sensor deployment or customer savings. Site-specific testing is required before treating any optical estimate as a calibrated parameter. Continuous monitoring Can UV/Vis sensors monitor industrial wastewater continuously instead of lab samples? For process control, yes. For compliance, no. An in-line UV/Vis instrument reads the stream continuously, so it can show a change in the water long before a grab sample reaches the lab. It does not replace the sample, the reference method or the lab report wherever a permit or approved procedure requires them. Lab results stay authoritative for compliance limits. Four conditions decide whether a continuous optical signal is useful at a given plant. Calibration is site-specific. A generic or vendor calibration does not carry over to an unfamiliar effluent. Paired lab samples from the plant's own water are needed before an optical reading is treated as an estimate of any parameter. Fouling needs a maintenance routine. Film on the optical window, scattering from suspended solids and bubbles all shift the signal. Cleaning intervals and quality checks have to be set and followed, or drift will look like a process change. Interferences change the reading. Suspended particles, temperature and changes in the mix of constituents all affect absorbance. The analysis has to separate them from a real change in the process stream. BOD is the only parameter AquaMesh calibrates. It is calibrated against the plant's own reference samples and validated blind before anyone relies on it. Everything else AquaMesh reports from the spectrum is spectral change analysis. It shows that the water changed, not a certified concentration. In practice, the continuous signal tells an operator when to look and where to sample. AquaMesh recommends a check and the operator decides; it does not actuate equipment. Read more about spectral change detection versus calibrated parameters . Direct answer What does combining spectroscopy with AI actually do? UV/Vis spectroscopy and AI serve different roles. A spectral instrument records wavelength-dependent light absorption in a sample or process stream. Depending on the instrument and application, that signal may reveal changes in dissolved constituents or suspended material. The process model combines the optical signal with existing data such as flows, valve states, batch changes, conductivity, temperatures, and laboratory samples. It then tests likely causes, estimates an operating consequence, routes a recommendation to an operator, and checks the subsequent result. It does not automatically identify every chemical, produce a regulatory BOD or COD measurement, or prove that a process change caused a loss. The physical measurement, model and operational decision each need separate validation. For a plant that already has sufficient instruments, the right starting point is historian and SCADA analysis . Additional spectral sensing only makes sense when an existing measurement cannot resolve a valuable decision. How it works Five steps from water measurement to operating action. 1 Locate the loss or unstable condition Pick one operating question, such as product carryover during a cleaning transition or unexpected organic loading. Define which action would change if the condition were detected earlier. 2 Use existing tags before adding hardware Align historian, PLC, SCADA, production, maintenance and laboratory timestamps. Check units, sensor faults, equipment operating modes, and whether the signal already answers the question. 3 Measure a missing physical signal If ordinary conductivity, flow or sample data cannot distinguish product from rinse water, evaluate UV/Vis absorbance or another appropriate optical method at the decision point. NIR or Raman may be useful for different materials, but each has its own optical and deployment constraints. 4 Connect a change to its process context Compare the spectrum or derived indicator with recipe, changeover, valve and flow records. Rank plausible causes; quantify the opportunity using the site's own throughput, unit values and tariffs. Flag uncertainty instead of presenting a correlation as a diagnosis. 5 Verify an operator-approved response Present the evidence and proposed check to the responsible operator. After a permitted adjustment, compare the subsequent physical reading and production outcome against the expected result. Preserve an audit trail, including rejected recommendations. Two applications Where the combination matters. Food and beverage: product loss and clean-in-place (CIP) transitions Suppose a dairy or beverage plant changes from product to rinse water. The plant's PLC shows the changeover and routing valve, but a time-based recipe does not directly establish when the remaining product has cleared the line. A suitably validated optical trend at a return or drain point could be correlated with the valve sequence to test a narrower diversion interval. The analysis must distinguish product variation, entrained air, suspended particles, sensor fouling and cleaning chemistry before recommending a change. Financial value combines demonstrably recoverable product, water, energy and treatment charges, net of implementation cost. Industrial wastewater: unexpected organic load or treatment upset An optical trend may provide earlier evidence that the incoming water has changed than a delayed grab-sample result. Flow, tank levels, upstream production and aeration records help establish whether the change is operationally important and where it originated. A trend is not a certified BOD or COD result: site-specific paired samples, error bounds and the required reference method remain authoritative for compliance. Read more about spectral change detection versus calibrated parameters . Validation What must be proved before a plant relies on it? Instrument: establish the optical range and field stability, inspect fouling, scattering, bubbles, temperature effects and matrix variation; verify cleaning and maintenance intervals. Model: keep entire batches, recipes and operating periods out of training, then measure false alarms, missed events, drift and error against independently timed reference observations. Operating decision: show that an alert arrived before a real decision window closed, its suggested cause was investigated, and the action and result were independently verified. For BOD or COD estimation, do not inherit a vendor's generic calibration as proof for an unfamiliar effluent. In a six-plant study archived by EPA, wastewater-specific calibration improved the accuracy of UV/Vis estimates relative to broader models. USGS field guidance on fluorescence sensors, a related but distinct optical measurement method, also documents interference, maintenance and quality-control requirements. A laboratory result remains authoritative wherever the permit or approved procedure requires it. The purchase test is a decision, not a dashboard. If an existing historian tag reliably supports the same action, adding a spectral instrument is not justified. If the missing measurement changes an economically important decision, define the blind test and the maximum acceptable error before ordering hardware. Common questions Frequently asked engineering questions. Can UV/Vis spectroscopy measure BOD and COD directly? No. The instrument measures optical response. BOD and COD may be estimated through calibrated surrogate models for a particular water matrix. Performance can change with suspended particles, composition and operating conditions. Reference laboratory methods are still needed for calibration and any legally required reporting. Does a plant need an additional sensor to use AI optimization? Not necessarily. Much of the initial value can come from existing historian, SCADA, production and lab records. Add instrumentation only where a clear measurement gap prevents a consequential operating decision. How is this different from a conventional water quality dashboard? A dashboard reports instrument values and alarms. The proposed process model connects a developing condition to equipment state, likely causes, operational consequences, a named operator response and subsequent verification. The difference must be tested on real operating evidence rather than inferred from the interface. Does AquaMesh replace PLCs, SCADA or laboratory reporting? No. AquaMesh is designed as an advisory layer alongside existing controls and reference methods. The first step is read-only analysis; any future control integration must be separately approved and validated by the plant. References and scope Independent technical sources. Rieger, Langergraber Siegrist, Water Science and Technology (2006), indexed by U.S. EPA : UV/Vis wastewater calibration study; establishes the importance of wastewater-specific calibration. Water Research (2016), calibration of UV/Vis spectrophotometers : compares calibration approaches and model performance for TSS and COD estimation in sewers, treatment plants and rivers. U.S. Geological Survey, Techniques and Methods 1-D11 : optical instrument selection, interference, cleaning and quality assurance for fluorescence measurements. U.S. Geological Survey, Open-File Report 2026-1063 : turbidity corrections and verification considerations for fluorescent dissolved organic matter (fDOM) sensors. These sources support general measurement cautions; they are not independent validation of AquaSpectra or AquaMesh. AquaMesh's industrial spectral instrument and any site-specific BOD model require validation before performance claims can be made. Start with a decision your plant cannot make soon enough. We can examine the process, existing records and the cost of that blind spot before deciding whether optical sensing is needed. TITLE: Cooling tower blowdown control: conductivity drift cost
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/cooling-tower-blowdown-conductivity-sensor-drift.html
DATE: 2026-10-28
SECTION: Measurement
TAGS: cooling tower, blowdown, conductivity, water efficiency, industrial water management
==============================================================================

Cooling tower blowdown is controlled by a conductivity setpoint. When the circulating water reaches a programmed conductivity level, the blowdown valve opens and a portion of the basin is discharged. The logic is straightforward: conductivity rises as dissolved solids concentrate through evaporation, and the setpoint represents the maximum concentration the system is designed to run at before dumping water and replacing it with fresh makeup.

The measurement doing that work is a conductivity sensor in the basin or blowdown line. If that sensor reads high, the control system discharges water that was still within operating range. If it reads low, the system lets concentration climb beyond the setpoint before triggering blowdown. Either failure mode costs money, and neither is visible until it shows up in water bills or on heat exchangers.

## How conductivity blowdown control works

A conductivity sensor in the basin or blowdown line reads dissolved solids continuously. A controller compares that reading to a programmed setpoint corresponding to the design cycles of concentration (COC). When the reading crosses the setpoint, the blowdown valve opens and fresh makeup water replaces what was discharged. The system is designed to run at the highest COC the water chemistry can sustain, since higher COC means less water discarded per unit of cooling output. The DOE Federal Energy Management Program documents a 20 percent reduction in makeup water and a 50 percent reduction in blowdown when moving from 3 to 6 COC -- a difference controlled entirely by where the sensor's reading lands relative to actual basin concentration. ([DOE FEMP Best Management Practice #10: Cooling Tower Management](https://www.energy.gov/femp/best-management-practice-10-cooling-tower-management))

**How to detect conductivity sensor drift before it accumulates cost:**

1. Cross-check with a calibrated handheld meter at each maintenance visit. A divergence of more than 5 percent means the loop measurement should not be trusted to control blowdown until recalibrated.
2. Pull blowdown valve timestamps and conductivity readings from the historian for a rolling 60-day window. Rising event frequency with stable makeup water quality points to the sensor, not the process.
3. Track blowdown events normalized to cooling load. Fouling-driven high-bias drift appears as more blowdown events per unit of heat rejection over time, with no change in ambient conditions or system load to explain it.
4. Compare makeup water conductivity readings over the same period. If makeup quality is stable and blowdown frequency is rising, the sensor or the controller setpoint has changed -- not the incoming water.

## Why cycles of concentration are the performance metric

The conductivity setpoint corresponds directly to cycles of concentration: the ratio of dissolved solids in the circulating water compared to the makeup water. At three cycles of concentration, the circulating water is three times as concentrated as the incoming makeup. At six cycles, it is six times as concentrated, meaning the system has extracted six times the evaporative cooling work from each unit of water before discharging it.

The Department of Energy's Federal Energy Management Program, in its Best Management Practice for Cooling Tower Management, documents the consequence of that difference: increasing cycles from three to six reduces cooling tower makeup water consumption by 20 percent and cooling tower blowdown by 50 percent. ([DOE FEMP Best Management Practice #10: Cooling Tower Management](https://www.energy.gov/femp/best-management-practice-10-cooling-tower-management))

Most cooling towers run at two to four cycles of concentration. The practical ceiling is set by water chemistry: calcium, magnesium, silica, and other dissolved minerals will eventually scale heat exchange surfaces or corrode metal components if concentration runs too high. Water treatment programs add scale inhibitors and corrosion inhibitors specifically to allow higher cycles of concentration without those chemistry problems. But there is a second constraint that receives less attention: the accuracy of the conductivity measurement that tells the system what concentration it is actually running at.

## What sensor drift does to blowdown frequency

Conductivity sensors in cooling tower service face a corrosive environment. Basin water contains biological growth, suspended solids, scale-forming minerals, and treatment chemicals. Sensor fouling from biofilm and mineral deposits is the most common failure mode, and the most common direction of failure is a reading that drifts high: a deposit on the sensor surface creates an impedance that the controller interprets as elevated dissolved solids in the water.

A sensor reading high produces the same control response as actual high concentration: it triggers blowdown. If the setpoint is 1,500 microsiemens per centimeter and the sensor reads 1,600 when the actual basin conductivity is 1,200, the controller sees an out-of-spec condition and opens the valve. The water being discharged was at 1,200 microsiemens, well within the setpoint, and capable of running through additional evaporative cycles before requiring blowdown.

This is not a hypothetical edge case. Sensor fouling accumulates gradually, and in many plants the cleaning interval for conductivity sensors is set by a calendar schedule rather than by measurement-to-measurement agreement. A sensor cleaned monthly in a high-load summer period is operating for weeks with accumulating offset. During that interval, every blowdown event the offset triggers is water the system did not need to discharge.

The reverse failure also occurs: a sensor that reads low because of a calibration shift or a failed element delays blowdown past the intended setpoint. Scale begins depositing on heat transfer surfaces, thermal performance drops, and in severe cases chemical treatment effectiveness falls as the system runs beyond its design envelope. Scale deposits of even 1/16 inch on heat exchanger surfaces can reduce thermal efficiency by roughly 10 percent. ([Rahmani et al., Applied Thermal Engineering, 2017, doi:10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2016.10.191](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1359431116341849))

## Quantifying the cost of over-blowdown

The DOE documents a 50 percent reduction in blowdown when moving from three to six cycles of concentration, and that figure provides a basis for estimating what premature blowdown costs. The calculation depends on facility size, local water costs, and sewer discharge fees, but the structure is consistent:

**At a facility with 1 million gallons per day of makeup water:**

| Operating scenario | Approximate daily makeup water | Approximate daily blowdown |
|---|---|---|
| 6 cycles of concentration (design intent) | 1,000,000 gallons | ~200,000 gallons |
| 3 cycles of concentration (sensor reads high) | 1,200,000+ gallons | ~400,000 gallons |
| Difference from premature blowdown | 200,000+ gallons/day | ~200,000 gallons/day |

*Modelled example using DOE FEMP documented percentage differences; actual values depend on evaporation rate, local water chemistry, and the degree of sensor offset.*

That makeup water difference carries three layers of cost. First, water purchase cost: industrial water rates vary by region, but an industrial facility paying in the range of $1 to $5 per thousand gallons for purchased water faces a material cost when hundreds of thousands of gallons per day are discharged unnecessarily. Second, sewer and wastewater discharge costs: many jurisdictions charge for cooling tower blowdown discharge separately from water purchase, and in areas with sewer surcharges for high-conductivity industrial discharge, this cost can approach or exceed the water purchase cost. Third, chemical treatment cost: every gallon of blowdown replaced with fresh makeup water requires treatment chemicals to protect the system from the new makeup water's chemistry.

For facilities that discharge cooling tower blowdown directly to surface waters, there is a fourth cost layer: regulatory exposure. Cooling tower blowdown discharged to waters of the United States requires authorization under the EPA's National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) program, and industrial discharge permits for many categories include limits on specific conductance or total dissolved solids as a proxy for concentrated minerals and treatment chemicals. A sensor reading low (allowing cycles of concentration to run above design) may produce a discharge that exceeds permit limits even when the control system appears to be operating normally, because the system registers a conductivity that is within setpoint while actual basin concentration has climbed past it. ([40 CFR Part 122, EPA NPDES Permit Regulations](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-122))

None of this is visible at the level of a single blowdown event. It becomes visible in trends: makeup water consumption trending upward over a season, chemical feed rates increasing without a corresponding change in makeup water quality, blowdown frequency in the historian rising faster than ambient temperature or load would predict.

## The diagnostic that is already in the historian

The same diagnostic approach that reveals DO sensor drift in aeration systems applies to conductivity sensor drift in cooling tower control. The data is in the historian: blowdown valve timestamps, conductivity sensor readings, makeup water flow, and any makeup water quality monitoring already being logged.

The signature of a sensor reading high is blowdown events that cluster at a conductivity reading just above the setpoint, while makeup water conductivity readings stay constant and blowdown event frequency increases over time on a consistent load. The signature of a sensor reading low is the opposite: infrequent blowdown with conductivity readings that stay below the setpoint even as the tower accumulates load, followed eventually by scale chemistry indicators or pressure-drop increases in the heat exchangers.

This is a temporal version of the spatial drift problem described in a parallel-equipment analysis. In that case, two identical aeration basins showed diverging blower runtime and energy use that reflected sensor offset rather than actual process differences. Here, the same principle operates over time in a single system: the measurement feeding the control loop has an offset, the loop acts on the offset rather than the process state, and the cost accumulates in the historian before it appears anywhere else.

The full parallel-basin methodology is in [why parallel equipment drifts apart, and what the gap costs](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html). For data centers where cooling tower blowdown directly affects the WUE metric, the connection between sensor drift and reported efficiency is covered in [data center WUE: what the metric measures, what it misses, and what it takes to move it](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/data-center-wue-measurement-gap.html).

## What accurate conductivity measurement enables

When the conductivity sensor controlling blowdown is reading accurately and corrected between calibration intervals, the control system can run the tower at the cycles of concentration the water treatment program was designed for. The 20 to 50 percent water savings the DOE documents from moving from three to six cycles are achievable without chemistry changes or capital investment -- they require that the measurement driving the control loop reflects actual basin conditions.

For industrial facilities with large cooling loads -- power generation, petrochemical, food and beverage processing, large manufacturing plants -- the difference between running at three cycles and six cycles is not a marginal optimization. At the scale of a 2,000-ton cooling tower system, it is a question of hundreds of thousands of gallons per day.

The diagnostic questions are straightforward. Is the conductivity sensor reading the same at the start and end of a calibration interval? Does blowdown frequency track makeup water conductivity the way it should, or does it drift independently? Are blowdown events triggering at the expected conductivity setpoint, or consistently below it? The answers are in the historian. The constraint is having a way to pull the data at the resolution that shows blowdown-event-level behavior over a long enough window to separate sensor drift from process variation.

---

If your cooling tower water use has trended upward or your blowdown frequency looks inconsistent with your system load, the control data is already in your historian.

See what a water system measurement review looks like at an operating industrial facility: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant case study](https://aquamesh.ai/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html). Or [reach out to schedule a working session with the team](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).

TITLE: In Water Online: the $1.5 million sewer repair and the water-quality evidence missing upstream
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/water-online-sewer-repair-evidence.html
DATE: 2026-10-26
SECTION: In the press
TAGS: industrial wastewater, pretreatment, discharge compliance, sewer surcharges, spectral sensing, Water Online
==============================================================================

Water Online published a guest column by Alex Towfigh, AquaMesh's founder and CEO, on 26 October 2026. The full piece is on the Water Online site: [The $1.5 Million Sewer Repair — And The Water-Quality Evidence Missing Upstream](https://www.wateronline.com/doc/the-million-sewer-repair-and-the-water-quality-evidence-missing-upstream-0001).

What follows is a short summary.

## The argument in brief

**The case.** A California wire manufacturer was ordered to pay $1.5 million in restitution after acidic wastewater damaged a public trunk sewer. EPA's 2010 announcement described 14 illegal discharges over four months of 2008, with pH as low as 1 against a permit minimum of 6. The column is careful about what this shows: the restitution covered cumulative damage, and a new analyzer alone would not necessarily have stopped the discharges. Its question is whether the plant could have recognized a repeated pattern early enough to investigate the treatment system behind it.

**An endpoint is not an explanation.** A pH probe at the discharge point tells you whether neutralization worked. It does not tell you whether the cause was a transfer, a dosing fault, a bypass, a reagent shortage or maintenance. Better detection cannot replace working treatment equipment, but it can shorten the path from a suspect reading to its cause.

**Two bills for the same discharge.** Lost product and treatment surcharges are separate ledgers, and the column warns against counting the same saving twice. It works through a dairy scenario using a published loss range of 1% to 3% of milk processed, and a COD example using San Diego's published January 2026 rate of $0.27 per pound: at 1 million gallons a day with 1,000 mg/L of added COD, about $2,252 a day. Both are sensitivity calculations, not measured losses or billing forecasts, and the column says so.

**The blind spot between systems.** Read-only access to PLC, SCADA and historian data reconstructs what production was doing and when. A multiwavelength UV/visible sensor can show changes in the stream that pH, flow or conductivity miss, provided it is calibrated on site. A rinse that lines up with an optical change is a lead to check against a lab sample, not a finding.

**The clock decides usefulness.** Detection only helps if it arrives in time to act. EPA event-detection research found that many unexpected water-quality changes came from operational changes or sensor problems rather than contamination. So the measures that matter are lead time, confirmed causes, false alerts per shift and cost, not anomaly accuracy on its own.

## Three questions for the next operations meeting

For each recurring discharge, the column asks:

1. What is the earliest validated water-quality measurement?
2. Which upstream records would explain it?
3. What authorized operating change would prevent it from happening again?

It closes with a test of its own: find the single missing measurement that would most improve the conclusion. If there isn't one, more sensors may not be the right investment. And AquaMesh's value has to be shown the same way, through lower confirmed losses, earlier diagnosis or less investigation effort.

[Read the full column in Water Online](https://www.wateronline.com/doc/the-million-sewer-repair-and-the-water-quality-evidence-missing-upstream-0001).


==============================================================================
TITLE: Intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal: what DO sensor precision actually controls
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control.html
DATE: 2026-10-23
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: nitrogen removal, intermittent aeration, dissolved oxygen, SND, wastewater treatment
==============================================================================

Biological nitrogen removal is one of the more demanding process control challenges in activated sludge treatment. Plants with tight effluent nitrogen limits need to run two competing biological processes: nitrification under aerobic conditions and denitrification under anoxic ones, efficiently, in the same biological system. For plants using intermittent aeration to accomplish this in a single-basin configuration, the precision of dissolved oxygen control during aeration cycles is not an instrumentation detail. It is the variable that determines whether the strategy works.

## What intermittent aeration is trying to do

Conventional biological nitrogen removal stages aerobic and anoxic zones in sequence: ammonia is nitrified to nitrate in an aerated zone, then denitrified to nitrogen gas in a downstream anoxic zone. The system is reliable but capital-intensive and requires careful hydraulic design.

Intermittent aeration takes a different path: the same basin alternates between aerobic and anoxic phases by cycling blowers on and off. During the aerated phase, nitrifiers convert ammonia to nitrate. During the unaerated phase, denitrifiers reduce nitrate to nitrogen gas, using carbon already present in the mixed liquor. Some organisms can carry out both reactions near-simultaneously at low dissolved oxygen concentrations, a phenomenon called simultaneous nitrification-denitrification (SND). The EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual identifies low-DO operation, typically below 1.0 mg/L, as a condition that promotes SND in conventional activated sludge by creating anoxic microsites within biological flocs. ([EPA, Nutrient Control Design Manual, 2010, Section 5](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2019-08/documents/nutrient-control-design-manual.pdf))

A 2022 review in Chemical Engineering Journal analyzed over 50 intermittent aeration studies and found that precise DO control during aeration phases was the most consistent predictor of nitrogen removal efficiency, ahead of cycle length or influent carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. ([Miao et al., 2022, Chemical Engineering Journal, doi:10.1016/j.cej.2021.133516](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1385894721047604))

The practical appeal is real: intermittent aeration can achieve substantial nitrogen removal without a separate anoxic zone, with lower aeration energy than continuous-aeration systems, and with flexible response to variable influent loads. These advantages depend on cycle timing, and cycle timing depends on DO measurement.

## Where DO control precision comes in

The cycle timing in intermittent aeration is almost always governed by a dissolved oxygen setpoint rather than a fixed timer. Aeration turns on when DO falls below a lower bound; it turns off when DO rises above an upper bound. The accuracy of that DO band controls the effectiveness of the strategy:

**Sensor reading low (common fouling failure):** A sensor that reads 0.4 mg/L when actual DO is 1.8 mg/L keeps blowers running long past the point where nitrification has completed. The aerobic phase extends beyond the design intent. The anoxic fraction shrinks. Denitrification suffers, nitrogen removal drops, and the plant uses more electricity than the intermittent strategy was supposed to require.

**Sensor reading high:** Aeration shuts off early. The basin does not complete nitrification in one cycle. Ammonia carries over. In a plant with a permit nitrogen limit, this is an effluent compliance risk, not just an energy problem.

**Fouling that accumulates between cycles:** Mixed liquor accumulates on membrane or optical sensor surfaces during the unaerated phase. When aeration restarts, the sensor enters the aerobic phase with an offset that compounds over successive cycles if cleaning intervals are not calibrated to match actual fouling rates.

The cumulative effect is that the DO setpoints operators specify on the control screen may not correspond to the dissolved oxygen concentration the organisms experience. The blower control loop optimizes against a sensor output, not against the process state.

## What this looks like in practice

The same phenomenon described in the parallel-basin aeration analysis applies here in a temporal rather than spatial dimension. In that case, two basins running simultaneously showed a DO divergence that reflected sensor drift rather than process differences: one blower was pinned at maximum output, consuming over $3,000 per year more than its twin, for the full 25-day record. The spatial version was visible by comparing basins side by side. The parallel equipment drift analysis is in [why parallel equipment drifts apart](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html), and the full historian data methodology is in [what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html).

The temporal version in intermittent aeration requires a different analysis: charting DO sensor output against blower on/off timestamps at five-minute or finer resolution, and comparing aerobic phase duration over time. A sensor reading accurately produces aerobic phases of consistent duration for a given influent load. A sensor that is drifting produces phases that systematically lengthen (reading low, blowers run long) or shorten (reading high, blowers cut off early) in ways that do not track influent load changes.

Both versions share the same root cause: the measurement feeding the control loop has an offset that the loop cannot self-detect, because there is no independent reference running alongside it.

## The energy calculation for intermittent aeration

The aeration energy baseline for secondary treatment, around 1,500 kWh per million gallons for activated sludge, assumes reasonably continuous aeration. Intermittent aeration in a nitrogen-removal configuration typically aims to reduce aeration runtime to 50 to 70 percent of total time, depending on the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the influent and the cycle design. That would imply aeration energy in the range of 750 to 1,050 kWh per million gallons when timing is accurate.

At a 10 MGD plant and the current EIA industrial rate of $0.0977 per kWh ([EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a)), the difference between accurate intermittent aeration (approximately 900 kWh/MG as a midpoint) and sensor-extended aeration (1,500 kWh/MG because the sensor is holding blowers on too long) is approximately $215,000 per year at that scale.

**Modelled example for a 10 MGD plant with intermittent aeration:**

| | Accurate DO control | DO sensor drifting low |
|---|---|---|
| Aeration runtime share | 60% | 100% (effectively continuous) |
| Estimated kWh/MG | 900 | 1,500 |
| Annual energy cost at $0.098/kWh | $193,100 | $321,900 |
| Annual cost difference | | $128,800 |

This is a modelled example using published benchmarks; actual values depend on plant-specific loading, cycle design, and the degree of sensor offset. The direction is consistent: sensor drift in an intermittent aeration system does not only affect nitrogen removal performance. It erodes the energy savings that justified the intermittent strategy in the first place.

## What accurate DO measurement enables

When DO measurement in an intermittent aeration system is continuous, accurate, and corrected against drift between calibration intervals, the control loop can do what it was designed for: maintain the aerobic-to-anoxic balance that both nitrification and denitrification require.

For plants approaching permit limits on total nitrogen, the margin for process error is narrow. A sensor that introduces a systematic offset into the timing of aeration cycles is a measurement problem that manifests as an effluent compliance risk. The issue is usually visible in the historian data before it appears in the permit reporting: aerobic phase durations extending over time, DO baseline at cycle start gradually increasing, nitrogen removal efficiency declining in ways that do not correlate with influent load.

The diagnostic questions are the same ones that apply to continuous aeration systems. Are the DO sensors reading accurately between calibrations? Does blower runtime at a given influent load match what the setpoints predict? Are cycle times stable, or are they drifting? The methodology for that analysis is in [aeration energy at wastewater plants: the cost, the waste, and the measurement gap](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/aeration-energy-cost-wastewater-plants.html).

None of this analysis requires new hardware. The data is in the historian. The constraint is having a way to extract it at the resolution that shows cycle-level behavior, over a long enough window, against a reference that was not subject to the same drift.

---

If your plant uses intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal and you want to understand whether your DO control is performing as designed, the place to start is the cycle data already in your historian.

See what that review looked like at an operating plant: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant case study](https://aquamesh.ai/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html). Or [reach out to schedule a working session with the team](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).
