==============================================================================
TITLE: Data center WUE: what the metric measures, what it misses, and what it takes to move it
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/data-center-wue-measurement-gap.html
DATE: 2026-10-22
SECTION: Measurement
TAGS: data centers, WUE, water efficiency, cooling tower, water monitoring, water usage effectiveness
==============================================================================

Water Usage Effectiveness, or WUE, has become the standard headline number for data center water efficiency. It is reported in sustainability disclosures, cited in regulatory proceedings, and used in site-selection discussions in water-stressed regions. The formula is simple: liters of water consumed at a facility divided by kilowatt-hours delivered to IT equipment.

What WUE does not tell you is where the water is going, what is controlling it in real time, or whether the sensors responsible for that control are working. That is a separate question, and the answer to it determines whether a WUE target is achievable or theoretical.

## What WUE actually measures

The metric was introduced by The Green Grid, the data center industry consortium, as a companion to PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Like PUE, it is a ratio: lower is better and zero is the theoretical ideal. A site with a WUE of 2.0 consumes two liters of water for every kilowatt-hour its servers use.

Research on actual facility performance puts the range between 1 and 9 liters per kilowatt-hour depending on cooling approach, climate zone, and facility age, with a central tendency around 1.5 to 2 L/kWh for older evaporative cooling installations. ([Mytton, D. "Data centre water consumption." npj Clean Water 4, 52 (2021)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-021-00101-w)) Newer hyperscale builds using advanced chemistry management or closed-loop cooling report considerably lower values.

WUE is typically calculated annually. Some operators report quarterly. It is a useful benchmark for comparing facilities against each other and tracking long-run progress. It is a poor guide for what to do on Tuesday.

## Where the water actually goes

For facilities using evaporative cooling towers, which covers the majority of installed capacity, the water balance has two main terms: evaporation and blowdown.

Evaporation is the productive part. The cooling process works by letting water absorb heat and leave the tower as vapor. Roughly 70 to 80 percent of the water that enters the tower in this way is not recoverable; it has done its job and left the site. ([Mytton 2021](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-021-00101-w)) This fraction tracks the heat load on the facility and varies with ambient wet-bulb temperature. A site cannot significantly reduce evaporative losses without changing the physics of how it cools its equipment.

Blowdown is different. As water circulates through the tower and a portion evaporates, the dissolved minerals left behind concentrate. Calcium, silica, chlorides, and biological material accumulate. If concentration rises too high, scale deposits on heat exchanger surfaces and corrosion accelerates. To prevent this, some fraction of the circulating water is periodically discharged and replaced with fresh makeup water. That discharge is blowdown.

The ratio of dissolved mineral concentration in the circulating water to the concentration in the makeup supply is called the cycles of concentration. At three cycles, for every gallon that evaporates, roughly half a gallon is discharged as blowdown, and one and a half gallons are drawn in as makeup. At six cycles, blowdown drops to roughly one fifth of the evaporation volume. At ten cycles, it drops to one ninth.

**Modelled example:** For a 10-megawatt IT load facility with a moderate WUE of 2.0 L/kWh operating at 85 percent utilization, annual water consumption is roughly 149 million liters. If evaporation represents 75 percent of that total, the remaining 37 million liters per year is blowdown. Moving from 3 to 6 cycles of concentration reduces that blowdown component by approximately 60 percent, or 22 million liters per year. This is a modelled estimate based on the ratios above; actual results depend on makeup water chemistry, heat load profile, and seasonal variation.

## The measurement problem

The control system that manages blowdown uses a conductivity sensor as its primary input. Conductivity in the circulating water rises as dissolved minerals concentrate, and the controller uses this as a proxy for cycles of concentration. When conductivity reaches a set threshold, the blowdown valve opens and makeup water flows in.

This means the conductivity sensor, sitting in a basin or on a sidestream line, is the direct operational driver of water efficiency performance. A sensor that reads accurately and holds its calibration enables tight control at higher cycles. A sensor that has fouled, drifted, or been calibrated infrequently has the opposite effect.

A sensor reading low when concentration is actually high causes the controller to keep the blowdown valve closed longer than intended. Dissolved solids accumulate beyond design limits. Scale risk increases and the operator may not know it until a heat exchanger inspection. A sensor reading high when concentration is actually normal causes the controller to open the blowdown valve prematurely and repeatedly, discharging good water and drawing in fresh makeup water unnecessarily. The facility's WUE is higher than it needs to be, and the cause does not appear in the annual report.

Neither failure mode triggers an alarm in a standard building management system. The control loop is running. The conductivity reading is within the operating range. The controller is doing exactly what it was programmed to do with the signal it receives.

This is the same silent failure pattern that affects dissolved oxygen control in wastewater aeration basins, where a fouled sensor drives blowers toward wasted energy rather than toward needed oxygen. The structure of the problem is identical: a lagging indicator (WUE for water, energy per gallon treated for wastewater) does not point to the sensor drift that is the actual cause. The gap shows up only when you look at the control inputs directly, not at the outcomes they produce. The parallel is covered in more detail in the analysis of [why parallel equipment drifts apart](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html). It also applies to intermittent aeration cycles for nitrogen removal, where DO sensor drift affects both effluent compliance and the energy savings the intermittent strategy was meant to deliver: [intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal: what DO sensor precision actually controls](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control.html).

For a detailed breakdown of what conductivity sensor drift costs in cooling tower water volume and chemical spend, including a worked example using DOE benchmark data, see [cooling tower blowdown control: what conductivity sensor drift costs in water and chemicals](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/cooling-tower-blowdown-conductivity-sensor-drift.html).

## The California compliance context

California's AB 2619, signed in September 2026, requires data center operators to report total and direct annual water use by source at every business license renewal, under penalty of perjury. AB 2469 requires a Water Scarcity Plan by 2028 for facilities requiring construction permits. ([California data center water reporting requirements](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/california-data-center-water-reporting.html))

A Water Scarcity Plan is a commitment to reduce water consumption under specified drought conditions, including staged curtailment and targeted reductions by use type. The commitment is credible only if the site can demonstrate that it knows where its water goes and can reduce specific uses on demand.

A site operating at three cycles of concentration because its conductivity sensors drift between maintenance intervals cannot reliably commit to operating at six cycles under drought conditions. The chemistry that makes six cycles safe to operate requires measurement quality that makes four and a half cycles the actual operational average. The gap between the plan and the operational reality is a sensor reliability problem, not a strategy problem.

## Three questions worth checking before setting a WUE target

Before writing a WUE improvement target into a sustainability report or a Water Scarcity Plan, three questions are worth answering from existing historian data.

**What are your actual cycles of concentration, by tower?** This is calculable from makeup flow, blowdown flow, and conductivity readings. If the number is consistently below design, the control logic or the sensor driving it is worth examining before adjusting targets.

**How does blowdown volume correlate with wet-bulb temperature?** Evaporation tracks ambient conditions predictably. Blowdown should not spike independently of heat load. Unexplained blowdown events in the historian are almost always sensor artifacts or valve events, not chemistry responses.

**What share of total water use does blowdown represent?** If blowdown is running above 30 percent of total consumption on a facility that should be operating at moderate cycles, the conductivity control system is not performing at design. This shows up in 12 months of metered data and does not require a new study to identify.

None of this analysis requires capital investment. The data exists in most historian systems. The constraint is usually having a way to look at it with enough resolution and the right reference points to distinguish signal from noise.

---

If your site is preparing for California's 2027 renewal requirements or developing a scarcity plan for 2028, the water balance question is worth addressing before the commitment is made, not after. AquaMesh can review the historian data that is already being collected and identify where the measurement gaps are.

See how this kind of analysis surfaced a $3,300 per year blower anomaly at a wastewater treatment plant: [what 25 days of historian data actually shows](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html). Or [reach out to schedule a working session](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).

*Alex Towfigh is a founder at AquaMesh.*


==============================================================================
TITLE: Wastewater aeration energy: cost and the measurement gap
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/aeration-energy-cost-wastewater-plants.html
DATE: 2026-10-21
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: aeration energy, wastewater treatment, dissolved oxygen, blower control, energy optimization
==============================================================================

Aeration is the single largest line on the electricity bill for most activated sludge wastewater plants. Aeration systems typically represent 50 to 75 percent of total electricity consumption at activated sludge facilities. The logical response is to install dissolved oxygen sensors, add variable frequency drives to blowers, and let a control loop do the rest. Many plants have done exactly that. Not all of them kept the savings.

Here is what the cost actually looks like, why the standard fix often falls short, and how to recover blower energy without adding hardware.

## How large the prize is

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported the national average industrial electricity rate at $0.0977 per kWh in July 2026, up from $0.0933 the prior year. ([EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a))

Secondary treatment activated sludge plants typically use between 1,200 and 1,800 kWh per million gallons treated. The EPA's water and wastewater energy management documentation cites a common benchmark near 1,500 kWh per million gallons for secondary treatment. ([U.S. EPA, Ensuring a Sustainable Future: An Energy Management Guidebook for Wastewater and Water Utilities](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-12/documents/guide_energymanagement.pdf))

**Modelled example for a 10 MGD secondary treatment plant:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Annual flow treated | 3,650 million gallons |
| Electricity at 1,500 kWh/MG | 5,475,000 kWh |
| Aeration share at 60% | 3,285,000 kWh |
| At $0.098/kWh industrial rate | $321,900/year |

This is a modelled example based on published benchmarks. Actual costs vary with load patterns, treatment configuration, equipment age, and the utility tariff in effect. The kilowatt-hours are the right order of magnitude; the dollar figure resolves once you pull an actual utility bill.

At this scale, a 20 percent reduction in blower energy is worth roughly $64,000 per year. The Florida Water and Pollution Control Operators Association published analysis in April 2026 showing that basic demand-based DO control typically reduces blower energy by 10 to 25 percent, and that PLC-optimized control can reach 20 to 40 percent. ([FWPCOA, "Demand-Based DO Control And Energy Optimization," April 2026](https://www.fwpcoa.org/content.aspx?page_id=5&club_id=859275&item_id=134074))

Those are compelling numbers. The problem is that they describe what the system saves when it is working as designed. The gap between the theoretical savings and what a plant actually captures and keeps is usually a measurement problem.

## Where the savings go

A DO control loop has three components: a sensor reporting the current dissolved oxygen level, a controller comparing that reading to a setpoint, and a variable frequency drive adjusting blower output. The logic is straightforward.

The sensor is the weak link.

Electrochemical membranes foul and require regular replacement. Optical sensors are more stable but still accumulate biofilm in mixed liquor. A sensor that reads 1.8 mg/L when the actual basin concentration is 3.2 mg/L signals the controller that the basin is under-oxygenated. The controller responds by running blowers harder. The plant pays for electricity that achieves nothing useful, and nothing in the system indicates anything is wrong.

The inverse failure is less common but more consequential: a sensor fouled in a way that reads artificially high causes the controller to back off blowers when DO is genuinely borderline, with the process instability that follows.

Both failure modes are silent. The control loop is running. No alarms fire. The historian records the sensor output without knowing it has drifted. Operators checking the dashboard see normal-looking DO values.

This is why many plants install DO control hardware and see strong early results followed by gradual erosion. The hardware is still there. The control loop is still active. But the measurement feeding it has drifted, and the loop is now optimizing against a wrong input.

## The parallel basin case

Plants with multiple aeration basins running in parallel face a compounding version of this problem. Sensors in different basins drift at different rates depending on local solids loading, position relative to diffusers, and how consistently each one gets cleaned. The basins may share a common air header, but if their DO sensors are reading different offsets, the blower outputs serving them will diverge in ways that reflect sensor drift rather than actual process differences.

We covered the mechanics and cost of this kind of hidden divergence in [why parallel equipment drifts apart](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html). The direct energy cost of an over-aerated basin shows up in blower runtime. The downstream cost in nitrogen removal performance, when an anoxic zone receives excess dissolved oxygen, is harder to price but real.

## What the historian data showed

When we analyzed 25 days of historian data from an operating plant earlier this year, one of the first findings was a DO-driven blower anomaly: one basin was running at more than three times the DO level of its parallel twin, with its blower pinned at maximum output, for the full duration of the record.

Both basins drew on the same shared air header. The control loop was functioning. The deviation was visible only by comparing the two basins side by side at hourly resolution. A daily manual grab from either basin, taken at a representative time, could easily have missed it.

The finding was worth $3,316 per year in direct blower power, plus the process risk from carrying excess oxygen into a downstream anoxic zone. It was already in the data. It just had not been looked at in this way. The full analysis is in [what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html).

## What accurate measurement changes

When DO measurement is continuous, accurate, and does not accumulate drift between calibration cycles, the control loop has what it was designed to work from. Blower output tracks actual oxygen demand rather than sensor artifacts. Setpoints can be tightened because operators are not building in a buffer to account for measurement uncertainty.

For plants running [intermittent aeration for simultaneous nitrification/denitrification](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control.html), the DO swing required is fast and narrow. The economics of that strategy depend entirely on measurement that responds quickly and without offset.

Some plants extend this further with online analyzers for ammonium or nitrate to feed an ammonia-based aeration control loop. Those instruments use a different measurement principle than a DO probe, and what they actually detect versus what they are marketed as measuring matters before you specify one. [Spectral change analysis versus calibrated parameters](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/spectral-change-analysis-vs-calibrated-parameters.html) covers the distinction.

Accurate measurement also creates a defensible record of what happened. When a plant documents savings for a utility incentive program or a regulatory report, both the baseline and current performance need measurement that holds up to scrutiny.

The same measurement-loop dynamic drives water waste in cooling towers, where a conductivity sensor reading high causes the system to discharge water still within operating range. The cost structure for that failure mode is in [cooling tower blowdown control: what conductivity sensor drift costs in water and chemicals](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/cooling-tower-blowdown-conductivity-sensor-drift.html).

## How to cut blower energy without new equipment

The FWPCOA analysis cited above documents 10 to 40 percent reductions in blower energy from demand-based DO control, compared to running blowers without feedback. Plants already running VFDs in manual mode, or with feedback loops that have not been recommissioned since original installation, often have most of that gap still available. The five steps below work in sequence; later steps depend on the earlier ones being in place.

**1. Verify DO sensor accuracy before adjusting any setpoint.** A setpoint change based on a drifted sensor moves the control loop to a different wrong reference. The first step is confirming what the sensor is actually reading, using a calibrated portable meter at different times of day and across the full diurnal load range, not just immediately after cleaning or calibration. This establishes whether subsequent steps are starting from an accurate baseline.

**2. Reduce the DO setpoint to the process minimum your permit allows.** Most activated sludge systems designed for BOD removal can sustain full nitrification at setpoints between 1.5 and 2.0 mg/L. The EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual (2010, Section 5) documents that nitrification in suspended-growth systems can proceed at dissolved oxygen concentrations as low as 0.5 mg/L, with typical operating setpoints higher to buffer for load variation. If your plant is running a legacy setpoint of 2.5 or 3.0 mg/L without a process reason for it, the difference is directly recoverable blower energy. ([EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual, 2010](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/nutrient-control-design-manual-full.pdf))

**3. Close the feedback loop if it is running open.** VFDs installed without an active PID loop holding them to a DO setpoint are often switched to manual by operators who found manual mode more predictable. An open-loop VFD captures some savings compared to a fixed-speed motor but none of the demand-following reduction that justifies the installation. Closing the loop requires that step 1 is true: the feedback signal has to be accurate, or the closed loop will chase measurement noise.

**4. Set blower discharge pressure to the minimum the diffuser system requires.** Discharge pressure setpoints are frequently established at commissioning and not revisited. Reducing header pressure in measured increments, while monitoring airflow distribution and DO response across the basin, identifies how much design margin was left in place. The installed blower manufacturer's pressure-power curve quantifies the energy difference for the specific unit; it should be in the plant files or is available from the manufacturer directly.

**5. Stage blower capacity to follow actual oxygen demand.** Running extra standby capacity continuously, or cycling blowers on a fixed time schedule regardless of load, keeps equipment running in inefficient operating regions. A staging sequence that adds or drops blower capacity based on measured demand keeps each running unit nearer its design point. For plants with multiple basins and a shared air header, [the parallel-basin divergence problem](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html) can mask whether staging is working as intended; blower runtime comparisons across basins are a useful check.

None of these changes requires new equipment. Steps 2 through 5 all depend on step 1 being correct, because a setpoint, a feedback loop, a pressure target, or a staging sequence that starts from a drifted sensor reading optimizes against the wrong input.

## Three questions worth asking before tuning the control loop

Before commissioning a new aeration control strategy or investigating why existing savings have eroded, three questions are worth answering directly from available data.

**Are the DO sensors reading accurately?** A comparison between sensor output and a calibrated handheld grab at different times of day, not just right after calibration, shows whether a sensor is holding its reading or drifting between service intervals.

**What does the blower run-time history show?** If blowers are running at sustained high output during periods when influent flow and temperature are moderate, the measurement feeding the control loop deserves examination before changing the control logic itself.

**Are parallel basins loading evenly?** Persistent divergence in blower output between basins handling equivalent loads is almost always a measurement issue. It rarely responds to setpoint adjustments alone.

None of these analyses requires new hardware. The data is usually in the historian. The constraint is having a way to look at it at the right resolution, over a long enough window, against the right reference.

---

If your plant is spending in the range described above, the measurement question is worth examining directly. An initial review of your historian data can show whether the control loop is working from accurate inputs and where the largest gaps are.

See how AquaMesh approached this analysis at a membrane bioreactor reuse plant: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant case study](https://aquamesh.ai/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html). Or [reach out to schedule a working session with the team](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).

*Alex Towfigh is a founder at AquaMesh.*


==============================================================================
TITLE: In Dairy Foods: why dairy plants still miss their most expensive process losses
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/dairy-foods-process-losses.html
DATE: 2026-10-12
SECTION: In the press
TAGS: dairy, product loss, CIP, spectral sensing, process water, Dairy Foods
==============================================================================

Dairy Foods published a contributed article by Alex Towfigh, AquaMesh's founder and CEO, on 12 October 2026. The full piece is on the Dairy Foods site: [Why dairy plants still miss their most expensive process losses](https://www.dairyfoods.com/articles/99452-why-dairy-plants-still-miss-their-most-expensive-process-losses).

What follows is a short summary. The article itself is exclusive to Dairy Foods.

## The argument in brief

**The losses happen during transitions.** Published research puts routine losses of milk to sewer at 1% to 3% of the milk a plant processes. Most of it leaves during startups, interruptions, shutdowns and rinses: short windows where the pipe contents change and someone has to decide where product ends and water begins.

**More tags do not fix a missing measurement.** Conductivity tells you something changed, but not how much product is in the line. A flowmeter tells you how much is moving, but not what it is. Lab results come back after the decision has been made. If the plant never measured the chemistry, software running on the historian has nothing to analyze.

**Spectral sensing helps, if it can be trusted.** An optical spectrum carries far more information than a single-variable sensor. But temperature, bubbles, solids and a fouled window all move the reading. Without local calibration, a dirty window can look like a product loss, so every reading needs a confidence level attached.

**Context decides what a signal means.** Rising conductivity is expected during caustic circulation and alarming during a product transfer. The article describes starting from data the plant already has (CIP steps, valve positions, lab results) to establish operating state, adding sensing only where a real blind spot exists, and producing an explanation of what changed and why rather than another generic alarm.

**Prove it one event at a time.** Start read-only. Existing controls and sanitation checks stay in charge. Pick one expensive event, measure its baseline, catch it earlier, change the decision, and verify the result. One peer-reviewed UHT cleaning study cited in the piece used phase-endpoint measurement to cut a cleaning sequence from 142 to 66 minutes and roughly halve its effluent.

The article's dollar figures are sensitivity calculations at an illustrative plant scale, not measured results at any named facility. It says so, and so do we.

[Read the full article in Dairy Foods](https://www.dairyfoods.com/articles/99452-why-dairy-plants-still-miss-their-most-expensive-process-losses).


==============================================================================
TITLE: California now asks data centers what they actually use, under penalty of perjury
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/california-data-center-water-reporting.html
DATE: 2026-10-01
SECTION: Regulation
TAGS: data centers, water reporting, AB 2619, AB 2469, cooling water, water reuse, California
==============================================================================

On 21 September 2026 the Governor of California signed [AB 2619](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB2619), now Chapter 437 of the 2026 Statutes, and [AB 2469](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB2469) alongside it. Between them they change what a data center operator in California has to be able to say about water, and when.

The reporting obligation is the part worth reading closely, because it is more specific than the coverage suggests.

## What AB 2619 actually asks for

AB 2619 works through the business license process rather than through a new permit. It sorts data centers into three types: Type I, or hyperscale, at more than 10,000 servers or more than 25 megawatts; Type II between 2 and 25 megawatts; and Type III below 2 megawatts.

At initial application, the operator gives the water supplier, and repeats on the license application form, a good faith estimate of expected water use, the anticipated source, and projected volume for the maximum day, the maximum month, and the average year.

At every renewal, the operator reports the preceding calendar year's annual water use (and here the statute is precise) "including total water use and direct water use," along with the cooling system type.

Direct annual water use is defined in the bill as:

> The volume of water withdrawn, delivered, or otherwise used onsite for data center operations, including cooling, sanitation, irrigation, and any other operational use, identified by source, including potable water, nonpotable water, or recycled water.

All of it under penalty of perjury.

Two things in that definition do the work. The first is *identified by source*: potable, nonpotable, recycled, broken out, not aggregated. The second is the split between total and direct, which means a single number off the utility bill does not satisfy the renewal requirement.

One correction worth making, because it has circulated widely: several summaries describe AB 2619 as requiring disclosure of *indirect* water use, meaning the water consumed generating the site's electricity. The enacted text does not define indirect use and does not require it. If you are scoping a compliance programme, scope it to what the statute says.

## What AB 2469 adds, and the 2028 date

AB 2469 operates on the other side of the counter. It applies to cities and counties approving discretionary or ministerial permits for data center construction or expansion that increases maximum peak water use, and it requires a Water Supply Assessment under [Water Code section 10910 et seq.](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=WAT&division=6.&title=&part=2.10.&chapter=&article=), projected water use and efficiency measures, workforce disclosures, and an undertaking that the applicant carries the full cost of any water conveyance, treatment, storage or distribution infrastructure the project needs.

Effective 1 January 2028, it also requires a Water Scarcity Plan. That plan has to set out measures for five named conditions: an abnormally dry year, and moderate, severe, extreme and exceptional drought years, including staged reductions, curtailment, recycling and reuse, thermal load reductions, and load shedding.

AB 2469 does not mandate closed-loop cooling. Some coverage says it does. It does not.

## The gap this opens

A Water Scarcity Plan is a commitment to cut consumption by a stated amount under stated conditions, written down in advance, in front of a permitting authority. Writing a credible one requires knowing two things that many sites do not currently know with any precision.

The first is where the water is going now, by loop and by source. Evaporative cooling, blowdown, makeup, sanitation and irrigation are different lines with different elasticities, and a site that only knows its total has no basis for saying which it would cut first.

The second is how far each one can be cut before something else breaks. Curtailment on a cooling tower usually means running at higher cycles of concentration: less blowdown, less makeup, and a circuit that is now closer to the scaling and corrosion limits of its own chemistry. Recycling and reuse, both named in the statute, move in the same direction. The water you keep in the loop is water whose composition is drifting.

That is the real operational content of a scarcity plan. It is not a reporting exercise, it is a commitment to run the plant closer to its limits on demand, and the plan is only as good as the site's ability to see what happens when it does.

## Where measurement earns its place

Volumes are a flow metering problem, and the renewal report in AB 2619 is largely a question of whether a site is instrumented well enough to break its own consumption apart by source. Many are not, and 2027's renewals will be the first time that shows up with a perjury declaration attached.

Composition is a different problem, and it is the one that decides whether a curtailment commitment is safe to make. A plant running higher cycles, or taking a recycled source that was not in the original design basis, is operating a water chemistry that moves. [Spectral change analysis](/blog/spectral-change-analysis-vs-calibrated-parameters.html) is a reasonable fit here precisely because it does not depend on having a calibrated panel for every constituent that might matter: it watches the spectrum for what is correlating with something the operator cares about, and flags when that relationship moves. BOD is the one parameter AquaMesh calibrates; the rest is change detection.

For sites that already have a few months of history in a historian, the first question is usually answerable from data that exists. [What 25 days of one plant's data showed](/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html) is a reasonable picture of what that kind of look turns up, and it was not a water reporting exercise: it was a cost exercise that happened to require knowing where things actually go.

Nothing in either bill requires a sensor. Both require a site to be able to answer questions about its own water that a surprising number of operators currently answer by estimate. The first renewals under AB 2619 will establish how much tolerance there is for that, and the 2028 scarcity plans will establish how much tolerance there is for a commitment that nobody has tested.

Operators working through what this means for an existing site can see how we approach [data center cooling water](/industries/data-centers.html), or start with an audit of the data already being collected. Understanding what the site's own WUE figure actually measures, and what it omits, is useful context before committing to a curtailment plan; [the measurement gap in data center WUE](/blog/data-center-wue-measurement-gap.html) covers that ground.


==============================================================================
TITLE: What a 25-day historian audit finds at a treatment plant
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html
DATE: 2026-09-30
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: historian data, wastewater energy, plant audit, SCADA, membrane bioreactor
==============================================================================

A 25-day export of a water reuse plant's historian located roughly $42,000 a year in recoverable losses without a site visit, new instruments, or a capital request. The main items were aeration energy running above the plant's own control targets, membrane scour airflow above the manufacturer's specific guidance, and pump cycling at more than twenty times the design rate.

That figure came entirely from the plant's existing SCADA archive: 1,001 tags, 7,172,532 recorded values, covering 28 June to 23 July.

![Audit summary page: no-capital savings, fully instrumented savings, design flow percentage, and effluent turbidity. Values tagged M are measured from SCADA; E means calculated with stated assumptions.](../assets/audit/fig1.jpg "The front page of the delivered audit. Values tagged **M** are measured straight from the plant's SCADA; **E** means we calculated them, and the assumptions are written down.")

## Why a historian export is enough to start

Almost every plant already records far more than anyone reads. A SCADA historian captures every tag on a schedule, forever, and the overwhelming majority of those tags are never looked at unless something breaks. The data is not the constraint. Attention is.

Three properties make that archive useful:

- **It is continuous.** A lab result describes one moment. A historian describes every moment, which is the only way to see a slope rather than a point.
- **It contains pairs.** Plants run parallel equipment, twin basins, duty and standby pumps, two membrane trains. Equipment built to do the same job under the same conditions should behave the same way. When it stops, that divergence is a measurement in itself.
- **It is already paid for.** No capital request, no procurement cycle, no installation window.

## The method

For each signal we model what normal looks like for that signal at that plant, rather than against a textbook range. Where the plant publishes its own operating ranges, most do on the weekly sampling schedule, those become the reference. A finding only counts as a finding if it sits outside the range the plant itself posts.

Then each item is priced, which is the part that decides whether anyone acts:

- Blower power from the isentropic relation, using measured airflow and measured discharge pressure
- Pump power from measured flow and head
- Runtime from historian totaliser deltas
- Everything converted to money using the plant's own tariff

Each line is labelled **measured** or **estimated**. Where it is an estimate, the assumptions are written down so the plant's own engineer can check the arithmetic rather than take a vendor's word for it.

## Normalizing findings by output

Absolute dollar figures tell you what an opportunity is worth at one plant at one tariff. Normalizing by output tells you whether a plant is already close to its floor or has structural headroom left.

Energy intensity is the standard metric. The [EPA's Energy Management Guidebook for Wastewater and Water Utilities](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-08/documents/wastewater-energymanagement.pdf) benchmarks conventional activated sludge with secondary treatment and UV disinfection at roughly 400 to 1,000 kWh per million gallons treated, depending on nutrient removal requirements. Plants with membrane bioreactors typically run higher, in the range of 2,000 to 4,000 kWh per MG, because continuous air scouring to keep membranes permeable adds a large fixed aeration load that conventional basins do not carry. Plotting a plant's measured intensity on that distribution answers a different question than the dollar figure alone: whether an opportunity is ordinary or exceptional for a plant of that type.

The same logic extends to chemical dosing. Chlorine, polymer, and coagulant dose all should track the flow or load passing through the relevant process step. Dose per unit volume, expressed as mg/L or lb per MG in US customary units, is the trackable metric. A flat chemical dose through wide seasonal flow variation shows up clearly in normalized form. Raw dose data measured in gallons of solution pumped per day hides both overdosing and load-proportional drift.

For the MBR plant in this audit, the actual flow rate is withheld to preserve anonymity. The calculation is the same at any plant: total kWh divided by total volume treated. One month of historian data plus a flow totaliser read is enough to place a plant on the EPA benchmark curve.

## What came out

### One basin running 3.6x above its own posted range

The plant's sampling schedule posts pre-air dissolved oxygen at 0.5 to 1.5 mg/L. Basin 2 sat right in that band, median 0.49 mg/L. Basin 1 held a median of 5.35 mg/L on every day of the record, roughly eleven times its twin, with its blower command pinned at 99.99%.

Both basins draw on the same shared air header. That detail is what turns this from a mystery into a maintenance task: if the air supply is common and the outcomes are not, the problem is in the split, a valve or a damper, not in the control strategy. Worth $3,316 a year in blower power, plus the nitrogen-removal risk: the [EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual](https://www.epa.gov/nutrient-policy-data/nutrient-control-design-manual) identifies dissolved oxygen intrusion into anoxic zones as a primary cause of denitrification inefficiency, since aerobic organisms outcompete denitrifiers at elevated DO concentrations.

{{diagram:twin-basins}} -- Both basins draw on the same air header, so the difference is in the split rather than the control strategy.

One caveat worth repeating: a fouled DO probe can sit on an offset and still respond to airflow. The reading gets verified against a calibrated handheld before anyone opens a valve.

### Membrane scour air above what the flux needed

Airflow tracked the permeate rate almost perfectly, R-squared of 1.00, at a ratio well above the manufacturer's specific-scour guidance. Trimming toward the guideline at the measured flux, using the controls already installed, came to $5,391 a year. That was the largest no-capital line on the list.

### Pumps starting every twenty-five seconds

Reclaimed water pumps were logging 13 to 28 starts an hour against a manufacturer guideline near six for pumps that size. One asset logged 143 in an hour, a start every twenty-five seconds.

Every start draws locked-rotor current and heats the windings far more than running does. The [DOE's Motor Systems guidance](https://www.energy.gov/eere/amo/motor-systems) documents the relationship between start frequency and insulation aging: permissible starts per hour depend on motor frame size and thermal class, and the typical industrial limit for motors in the fractional to ten-horsepower range is well below what this historian was recording. This is a control deadband adjustment, not a purchase, and it was quietly writing a bill in motors, starters, and contactors: about $3,500 a year.

### Sixteen of sixteen reuse totalisers frozen

Every irrigation zone has a volume totaliser. Not one of them changed in twenty-five days.

Until they record, nobody can demonstrate how much recycled water went to beneficial reuse rather than straight to disposal, which is exactly the number a reuse programme is judged on. A configuration fix rather than a purchase, and it unlocks roughly $7,300 a year.

## What it added up to

| | |
|---|---|
| Direct savings, no capital at all | **$42,050 / yr** |
| Including about 7 h/week of reporting time returned | **$58,428 / yr** |
| Fully instrumented | **$92,200 / yr** |

Two subtotals are kept deliberately apart: money that comes off a bill, and operator hours given back. The hours are real, but they are not money off a bill, so they never get folded into the first number.

![Opportunity table with every line flagged measured or estimated, including blower energy, scour air, pump cycling, totaliser restoration, RAS flow, predictive maintenance, and reporting automation.](../assets/audit/fig2.jpg "Every line labelled. The predictive-maintenance figure is built asset by asset from the plant's own run hours and start counts, not taken as a percentage of a maintenance budget.")

## How to run this at your plant

The same analysis works on any SCADA or DCS historian export. Six steps:

1. **Pull the export.** Three to six weeks covers most seasonal operating modes. IT can usually produce a CSV or Parquet pull from OSIsoft PI, Ignition, or a standard historian without a change request.
2. **Inventory the tags.** Group them by equipment and then by process zone. The goal is not to read all 1,000 tags. It is to find the parallel equipment pairs and the flow totalizers.
3. **Find the paired equipment.** Twin basins, duty and standby pumps, multiple filters or membrane trains all generate internal comparisons. A performance difference between units drawing on the same feed is a finding with the evidence already in the data. The mechanics of why parallel equipment diverges are covered in [why parallel equipment drifts apart](/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html).
4. **Check against the plant's own ranges.** The sampling schedule or operations manual usually publishes target ranges. A historian signal sitting outside those ranges is a priority flag, because the plant itself told you what normal looks like.
5. **Normalize by output.** Divide energy use by treated volume in kWh/MG and chemical dose by treated volume in lb/MG or mg/L. Plot each as a time series. A rising normalized trend over weeks or months indicates process drift that periodic grab sampling will not catch.
6. **Price each finding.** Blower and pump power from the isentropic relation or motor-rated amperage; chemical cost from unit price and dose rate; pump starts from the contactor log. Use the plant's own utility tariff. Label measured from estimated.

The sequence takes longer the first time. The second time, most of the work is steps five and six.

## The caveat that matters most

Everything above is priced on a residential time-of-use schedule blending to $0.362/kWh. At 406,610 kWh a year this plant is well past residential scale and would normally sit on a commercial schedule at roughly half that blended rate.

On a commercial tariff, the same physical savings are worth about half what is shown.

The kilowatt-hours are measured either way; only their price is in question, and one utility bill settles it. We put that on the front page of the report rather than in a footnote, because showing the range is worth more than picking the flattering end of it.

## What this does not tell you

A twenty-five day window in summer will not capture seasonal variation. Capital figures other than instrumentation are order-of-magnitude and need firming with quotes. And every number here is a ceiling that assumes the recommendation is actually implemented and then maintained: an identified opportunity, not a realised saving.

For context on the energy benchmarking side, the [wastewater aeration energy cost post](/blog/aeration-energy-cost-wastewater-plants.html) covers how to compare blower costs against facility-type benchmarks and what continuous DO monitoring changes about that math.

![The AquaMesh recommendations view: findings with severity, the action to take, the evidence tags and the annual value, with accept, resolve and dismiss on each card.](../assets/audit.jpg "The same findings in the platform, where they keep recomputing on a rolling window rather than ageing in a PDF. Plant name removed; everything else is the product as it ships.")

If your plant keeps a historian, the same exercise is available on your data. It needs an export and nothing else.

Read the full anonymised audit: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant](/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html).

==============================================================================
TITLE: Why parallel equipment drifts apart, and what the gap costs
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts.html
DATE: 2026-09-26
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: parallel equipment, pump duty, lead lag alternation, aeration, predictive maintenance
==============================================================================

The most reliable finding in plant data is also the simplest: two things built to do the same job, under the same conditions, that have stopped behaving the same way.

It is reliable because it needs no baseline, no model of correct operation, and no agreement about what good looks like. The two units are each other's reference. If one has drifted from the other, something changed, and that something usually has a cost attached.

## Why the control system will not tell you

A modern control system is very good at holding a value and raising an alarm when a limit is crossed. Divergence between two units is neither of those things.

Both units can sit inside every alarm limit while being nowhere near each other. A pump at 84% duty and its twin at 39% are both running. A basin at 5.35 mg/L and its twin at 0.49 mg/L are both aerated. Nothing is out of range in the sense the alarm system understands, so nothing fires, and the gap persists for years because it never presents as an event.

That is the gap worth watching, and it is visible in data a plant already records.

{{diagram:twin-basins}}

Neither trace is outside an alarm limit. Both basins are aerated, both are running, and nothing fires.

## The three shapes it takes

### Duty that never alternates

Lead and lag assets are supposed to swap. When the alternation is disabled, or was never configured, or was turned off during a commissioning problem and never turned back on, the lead unit accumulates all the wear.

Lead-lag alternation (a standard reliability practice described in the [EPA Primer for Municipal Wastewater Treatment Systems](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-09/documents/primer.pdf)) is designed to equalize wear across redundant assets and ensure the standby unit is exercised regularly. The standby that has not run in months is the one the plant will depend on when the lead finally fails.

In one plant's record, return-activated-sludge pumps showed 504 run hours against 232 in the same twenty-five days, and the lifetime counters showed the gap compounding: 44,299 hours against 30,953. The lead unit reaches overhaul years earlier than it needs to while the standby sits idle.

{{diagram:duty-split}}

Twenty-five days of run hours, and the lifetime counters behind them.

Lead-lag alternation costs nothing to enable. What makes this finding persuasive rather than theoretical is that the same plant's MBR blowers and permeate pumps *were* balanced, which marks it as an oversight on one asset rather than a design choice.

### A shared supply, unequally split

Twin basins on a common air header should see similar dissolved oxygen at similar load. When one sits far above the other with its blower command pinned wide open, the control strategy is not the problem: the air is not arriving where it is supposed to.

This one is cheap to investigate and cheap to correct, which is what makes it worth finding. A valve position or a damper, not a capital project.

Aeration typically accounts for 55 to 70 percent of a treatment plant's electricity consumption ([EPA Energy Management Guidebook for Publicly Owned Treatment Works](https://cfpub.epa.gov/si/si_public_record_report.cfm?Lab=NRMRL&dirEntryId=287471)). An air distribution imbalance between twin basins does not show up in the daily energy report: it shows up in blower run hours, and the cause is upstream of both. How that translates to operating cost is described in [aeration energy at wastewater plants](/blog/aeration-energy-cost-wastewater-plants.html).

### Instruments that no longer agree

Two turbidimeters on the same permeate stream, one reading a median of 0.11 NTU with a 90th percentile of 0.26, the other reading 0.14 and 2.12: three and a half times the plant's posted upper limit.

One of them is drifting. Until you know which, compliance decisions are resting on an instrument that cannot be fully trusted. The encouraging part, in that case, was that the true value looked excellent.

Dissolved oxygen instruments follow the same pattern. In activated sludge, a DO sensor reading above actual holds the blower on past the setpoint; one reading below actual cuts aeration short before the biology is satisfied. The process consequence of that divergence, particularly during intermittent aeration cycles for nitrogen removal, is covered in [intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal](/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control.html).

## Why frequent starts cost more than running

A related pattern worth naming on its own, because it is consistently underestimated.

Pumps are often judged on run hours. The more expensive variable is usually starts. Every start draws locked-rotor current several times the running current, and the heat goes into the windings. Motor thermal protection guidelines, as documented in the [DOE guide on improving pumping system performance](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2014/05/f15/improving_pumping_system_performance.pdf), establish typical starting limits for mid-size motors because inrush heat cannot dissipate faster than winding insulation allows. Manufacturer specifications typically put that limit at a handful of starts per hour.

In one record, reclaimed water pumps were logging 13 to 28 starts an hour. One asset logged 143 in a single hour: a start every twenty-five seconds. No alarm fired, because at no point was any pump outside its operating limits. It is a control deadband, and the bill arrives years later in motors, starters and contactors.

{{diagram:pump-starts}}

## How to look for it in your own data

You do not need a platform to start. With a historian export and a spreadsheet:

1. **List your parallel assets.** Anything with a twin: pumps, blowers, basins, trains, filters.
2. **Compare run hours over the same window**, and compare lifetime counters if you have them. A persistent ratio far from 1:1 is the signal.
3. **Count starts per hour**, not just runtime, and compare against the manufacturer guidance for that size of machine.
4. **For process variables, plot the pair on the same axis.** Not each against its limit: against each other. Divergence that holds for weeks is not noise.
5. **Check duplicates against each other.** Two instruments on one stream that disagree are telling you something regardless of which is right.

What you are looking for in every case is persistence. A transient divergence is operations. A divergence that holds for the whole record is a setting, a valve, or an instrument, and all three are fixable.

## Why this is where we start

When we read a plant's history, parallel equipment is the first thing modelled, because it produces findings that are concrete, cheap to verify, and hard to argue with. Nobody has to accept a model's opinion about what dissolved oxygen should be. They only have to accept that two basins on the same air header ought to look alike.

More on what a historian export produces: [what 25 days of data actually shows](/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html).


==============================================================================
TITLE: Spectral change analysis versus calibrated parameters
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/spectral-change-analysis-vs-calibrated-parameters.html
DATE: 2026-09-22
SECTION: Measurement
TAGS: UV-Vis, spectral analysis, BOD, COD, online water quality monitoring, surrogate parameters
==============================================================================

An online water quality analyser usually arrives with a list: COD, BOD, TSS, nitrate, TOC. The list is the product. The implication is that the instrument measures each of those things the way a lab measures them, only continuously.

That is not how spectral measurement works, and the gap between how it is sold and how it behaves is where a lot of disappointment comes from.

## What the instrument actually produces

A UV/Vis probe does one thing: it measures how much light the water absorbs across a range of wavelengths, many times a second. What comes back is a curve, an absorbance spectrum. That curve is the raw measurement. Everything else is interpretation.

![UV/Vis and NIR absorbance spectra at clean, rising, high and very high loss, a reference fingerprint across 200-1700 nm, and spectral deviation from that reference.](../assets/starch-spectra.jpg "The raw measurement: absorbance across wavelength, many times a second. Everything downstream is interpretation of this curve.")

Converting that curve into "COD = 212 mg/L" requires a model that maps spectral shape to a lab value. Such models exist, they can be built, and for some parameters on some streams they are good. [ISO 15839](https://www.iso.org/standard/28624.html), which sets performance specifications for online water quality analysers, addresses this directly: models must be validated for the specific application, and performance characteristics may vary by site. In practice, this means the conditions that worked at one plant do not transfer automatically:

- They are often **site-specific**. Transferability must be demonstrated; a model validated on one stream should not be assumed valid on another.
- They **drift with composition**. Change the recipe, the season, the raw material or the upstream process, and the relationship between spectrum and lab value moves.
- They **degrade quietly**. A calibration that has stopped being right does not announce it. It keeps producing plausible numbers.

Without reference checks and maintenance, a parameter model can keep producing plausible numbers after its error has grown.

## The alternative: watch the spectrum move

There is a different use of the same hardware, and in a plant it is usually the more valuable one.

Instead of asking *what is the concentration*, ask *has the fingerprint changed, and what does that change correlate with*. Build a one-time model of what the plant's own stream normally looks like. Then watch for deviation from that reference, and tie the deviation to what the plant was doing at the time: feed rate, wash flow, machine state, cleaning records.

This is a materially easier question to answer well, and it is insensitive to the things that break calibrations:

- It does not need an absolute value, so it does not need to hold an absolute calibration
- It can handle defined operating modes more transparently when each recipe or season has an appropriate reference; new conditions still need review
- A drifting baseline shows up as drift rather than as a wrong number presented confidently

{{diagram:calibration-vs-change}} Same hardware, same spectrum, two different questions. Two very different maintenance burdens.

What you lose is the ability to report a concentration to a regulator. What you gain is a clear operating signal whose performance can be checked against current references over time.

## So why calibrate BOD at all

Because sometimes a number is the point.

Biochemical oxygen demand is the parameter that drives sewer surcharges, appears in [discharge permits under 40 CFR Part 133](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-N/part-133), and determines whether a load is going to cause a problem downstream. "The spectrum moved" is not an answer when the question is whether you are about to exceed a threshold that gets billed by the pound.

For the first industrial deployment, BOD is the parameter we plan to validate against the customer's own reference samples. The reference test is [Standard Method 5210B, as codified in 40 CFR Part 136](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-N/part-136). Their lab stays the method of record. The goal is to fill the hours between the samples the lab already takes, rather than replace them.

Other outputs begin as change analysis unless and until they are validated against an appropriate reference method.

## Why be this specific about it

Partly because it is true, and a claim that is not true gets found out in a technical review.

But mostly because the honest version is a better product story. "We measure sixteen parameters" invites a comparison against instruments from companies with thirty years of calibration work behind them, on a spec sheet, where we would lose. "We watch the whole spectrum for change and tell you what it correlates with in your plant, and we plan to validate BOD against your lab" is a different claim, and a parameter list does not answer it.

It also sets expectations that survive deployment. An operator who was told they were getting continuous COD and finds the number drifting stops trusting the instrument. An operator who was told they were getting an early warning that something in the water changed, and gets exactly that, keeps using it.

## What this means in practice

For a plant considering continuous optical measurement, three questions are worth asking any vendor:

1. **Which parameters are calibrated against my samples, and which are inferred?** The answer should be short and specific.
2. **What happens to the calibration when my feedstock changes?** If the answer is vague, assume it drifts.
3. **What is the instrument useful for if I never calibrate anything?** A good spectral instrument still earns its place as a change detector. A repackaged parameter list does not.

## Where this sits in the stack

Measurement is only half of it. A spectrum that moved is not an action: it becomes useful when it is correlated with plant state, attributed to a unit, and priced.

That is the division of labour: the probe reads the stream, the platform works out what the change means and what it is worth, and the operator decides what to do about it. What that process looks like against a real plant dataset is in [what 25 days of historian data actually shows](/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html). Working from a production historian to find cost events is the practical version of the correlation step described above.

More on what the sensor is used for by sector: [food and beverage](/industries/food-beverage.html), [industrial water](/industries/industrial-water.html), [pharma and biotech](/industries/pharma-biotech.html).
